title: One Protein, Two Grips: How Nuclear Receptors Wait

scenes.visual: Title card on deep slate background: 'One Protein, Two Grips: How Nuclear Receptors Wait' in clean crisp white (size 48). Below, a subtle animated schematic lipid bilayer pulses gently on the left as three small gold spheres drift lazily toward it.

scenes.tts: Most hormones knock at the cell surface and start a relay inside. What happens when a hormone slips straight through the membrane? Steroid hormones like cortisol and estradiol are hydrophobic, so they cross unaided.
scenes.caption: Most hormones knock at the cell surface and start a relay inside. What happens when a hormone slips straight through the membrane? Steroid hormones like cortisol and estradiol are hydrophobic, so they cross unaided.
scenes.visual: A cross-section of one schematic cell fills 70% of the frame height: plasma membrane on the left, cytoplasm in the center, nuclear envelope and pale cream DNA double strand on the right. First, a dim grey surface receptor receives a brief knock and fades out. Then gold steroid spheres glide smoothly straight through the lipid bilayer into the cytoplasm while the label 'Hydrophobic steroids cross directly' fades in at size 30.
scenes.narration: Most hormones knock at the cell surface and start a relay inside. What happens when a hormone slips straight through the membrane? Steroid hormones like cortisol and estradiol are hydrophobic, so they cross unaided.

scenes.tts: With no surface relay, the cell catches the hormone inside. One protein binds the hormone and grips D N A directly. A protein controlling whether genes copy into R N A is a transcription factor. Here, the receptor itself is that factor.
scenes.caption: With no surface relay, the cell catches the hormone inside. One protein binds the hormone and grips DNA directly. A protein controlling whether genes copy into RNA is a transcription factor. Here, the receptor itself is that factor.
scenes.visual: The gold sphere lands in a large teal receptor bar inside the cell. Two glowing arrows pulse on the single teal bar: one pointing to its rounded ligand pocket holding the gold sphere ('Binds ligand') and one pointing to its DNA-gripping teeth docking onto the cream DNA strand ('Binds DNA'). The DNA strand shimmers gently as a short RNA ribbon begins to sprout, labelled 'Receptor is the transcription factor' (size 30).
scenes.narration: With no surface relay, the cell catches the hormone inside. One protein binds the hormone and grips DNA directly. A protein controlling whether genes copy into RNA is a transcription factor. Here, the receptor itself is that factor.

scenes.tts: Humans have forty-eight nuclear receptor genes, and most share one modular plan. A ligand is the small molecule a receptor binds, like a hormone or lipid. One end carries a switching surface called A F one, and the other holds the ligand pocket. Between them, a domain folded around zinc reads D N A.
scenes.caption: Humans have 48 nuclear receptor genes, and most share one modular plan. A ligand is the small molecule a receptor binds, like a hormone or lipid. One end carries a switching surface called AF-1, and the other holds the ligand pocket. Between them, a domain folded around zinc reads DNA.
scenes.visual: The teal receptor bar expands smoothly across the center of the frame into four labelled segments (size 28+, no molecular structures): a warm orange block on the left ('AF-1'), a teal DNA-binding block containing two glowing amber dots ('2 zinc ions') reaching down to 6 highlighted ticks on the DNA strand, a flexible hinge bridge, and a larger teal pocket block on the right ('Ligand pocket + AF-2') enclosing a gold sphere. A small counter '48 human receptor genes' appears cleanly in the top-left corner.
scenes.narration: Humans have 48 nuclear receptor genes, and most share one modular plan. A ligand is the small molecule a receptor binds, like a hormone or lipid. One end carries a switching surface called AF-1, and the other holds the ligand pocket. Between them, a domain folded around zinc reads DNA.

scenes.tts: Most nuclear receptors work in pairs. Their site on D N A, called a response element, has two matching halves. Ligand binding and D N A binding sit in separate modules. So one protein links a signal directly to chosen genes.
scenes.caption: Most nuclear receptors work in pairs. Their site on DNA, called a response element, has two matching halves. Ligand binding and DNA binding sit in separate modules. So one protein links a signal directly to chosen genes.
scenes.visual: A second teal receptor glides in to pair side by side with the first above the cream DNA strand. Two bright 6-base blocks highlight along the DNA ('Half-site 1' and 'Half-site 2' with a short gap between them), labelled 'Response element' (size 30). Subtle brackets flash independently over the pockets ('Chooses ligand') and the zinc blocks ('Chooses gene') to show modularity.
scenes.narration: Most nuclear receptors work in pairs. Their site on DNA, called a response element, has two matching halves. Ligand binding and DNA binding sit in separate modules. So one protein links a signal directly to chosen genes.

scenes.tts: Before hormone arrives, how does a receptor wait? The family uses two routes. Glucocorticoid and androgen receptors wait mostly in the cytoplasm, held by H s p ninety chaperones. A chaperone holds a protein's shape, keeping the pocket ready and the receptor off D N A.
scenes.caption: Before hormone arrives, how does a receptor wait? The family uses two routes. Glucocorticoid and androgen receptors wait mostly in the cytoplasm, held by Hsp90 chaperones. A chaperone holds a protein's shape, keeping the pocket ready and the receptor off DNA.
scenes.visual: The frame splits smoothly into an upper lane ('Waiting off DNA') and a dimly lit lower lane ('Waiting on DNA'). In the upper lane, a teal glucocorticoid receptor sits in the cytoplasm wrapped by two slate-grey clamps labelled 'Hsp90 chaperones' (size 28). The clamps gently breathe in and out, holding the teal pocket slightly open while covering the zinc DNA-binding block so it stays away from the nucleus on the right.
scenes.narration: Before hormone arrives, how does a receptor wait? The family uses two routes. Glucocorticoid and androgen receptors wait mostly in the cytoplasm, held by Hsp90 chaperones. A chaperone holds a protein's shape, keeping the pocket ready and the receptor off DNA.

scenes.tts: When cortisol enters the pocket, the chaperone group rearranges. The receptor enters the nucleus and sheds its chaperones. Then it pairs with an identical copy on D N A. Estrogen receptors use the same chaperones, though most already wait inside the nucleus.
scenes.caption: When cortisol enters the pocket, the chaperone group rearranges. The receptor enters the nucleus and sheds its chaperones. Then it pairs with an identical copy on DNA. Estrogen receptors use the same chaperones, though most already wait inside the nucleus.
scenes.visual: In the upper lane, a gold cortisol sphere glides across the membrane into the teal pocket. The slate-grey Hsp90 clamps shift and stay loosely attached as the complex travels through a nuclear pore into the nucleus, where the clamps drift off. Two ligand-bound teal receptors pair up symmetrically and lock onto the two DNA half-sites. A small crisp note beside the nucleus briefly shows a second teal receptor with grey clamps already inside ('Estrogen receptor: chaperones in nucleus', size 28).
scenes.narration: When cortisol enters the pocket, the chaperone group rearranges. The receptor enters the nucleus and sheds its chaperones. Then it pairs with an identical copy on DNA. Estrogen receptors use the same chaperones, though most already wait inside the nucleus.

scenes.tts: Thyroid hormone receptors take a second route. They stay in the nucleus on D N A, paired with a partner called R X R. Picture an empty thyroid receptor on D N A without hormone. Is that gene at normal baseline, or quieter than with no receptor at all?
scenes.caption: Thyroid hormone receptors take a second route. They stay in the nucleus on DNA, paired with a partner called RXR. Picture an empty thyroid receptor on DNA without hormone. Is that gene at normal baseline, or quieter than with no receptor at all?
scenes.visual: The upper lane dims and the lower lane ('Waiting on DNA') brightens and expands. Inside the nucleus, a teal thyroid hormone receptor sits permanently on the cream DNA strand paired with an indigo-blue partner labelled 'RXR' (size 30). Its ligand pocket is visibly empty. A schematic transcription meter on the right shows a dashed 'Baseline' mark, with a glowing question mark hovering between 'Baseline' and 'Quieter than baseline'.
scenes.narration: Thyroid hormone receptors take a second route. They stay in the nucleus on DNA, paired with a partner called RXR. Picture an empty thyroid receptor on DNA without hormone. Is that gene at normal baseline, or quieter than with no receptor at all?

scenes.visual: Hold the empty teal thyroid receptor and indigo RXR on DNA with the question card at top center: 'Empty thyroid receptor on DNA: baseline or quieter?' (size 34). A subtle progress bar fills steadily across the bottom for 4.5 seconds while the question mark pulses gently.

scenes.tts: Even quieter, because the empty receptor holds a co-repressor, a helper that keeps the gene off. Co-repressors bring enzymes that strip acetyl tags from histones, the proteins D N A wraps around. The D N A packs tighter and blocks R N A polymerase, an active off switch.
scenes.caption: Even quieter, because the empty receptor holds a co-repressor, a helper that keeps the gene off. Co-repressors bring enzymes that strip acetyl tags from histones, the proteins DNA wraps around. The DNA packs tighter and blocks RNA polymerase, an active off switch.
scenes.visual: The schematic meter drops decisively below the dashed baseline into a coral-red zone labelled 'Active off (schematic)' (size 28). A coral-red block labelled 'Co-repressor' docks onto the empty teal receptor. Little green dots pop off three pale cream histone spools beneath the DNA, and the spools pull tightly together so a blocked RNA polymerase icon bounces away.
scenes.narration: Even quieter, because the empty receptor holds a co-repressor, a helper that keeps the gene off. Co-repressors bring enzymes that strip acetyl tags from histones, the proteins DNA wraps around. The DNA packs tighter and blocks RNA polymerase, an active off switch.

scenes.tts: When thyroid hormone binds, the receptor drops its co-repressor and recruits a co-activator. Co-activators add acetyl tags back to histones, loosening the D N A so transcription starts. Other family members sense lipids like fatty acids or bile acids. In this route, a nuclear receptor binds both ligand and D N A to control transcription.
scenes.caption: When thyroid hormone binds, the receptor drops its co-repressor and recruits a co-activator. Co-activators add acetyl tags back to histones, loosening the DNA so transcription starts. Other family members sense lipids like fatty acids or bile acids. In this route, a nuclear receptor binds both ligand and DNA to control transcription.
scenes.visual: A gold thyroid hormone sphere enters the teal pocket. The coral co-repressor detaches and floats away; an emerald-green block labelled 'Co-activator' snaps into place. Bright emerald acetyl dots attach to the histone spools, which glide apart smoothly to open the DNA as an RNA strand elongates and the schematic meter rises into green ('ON'). Small gold lipid icons briefly drift past ('Fatty acids · Bile acids', size 28) as the camera pulls back to show the full teal receptor bridging gold ligand and cream DNA.
scenes.narration: When thyroid hormone binds, the receptor drops its co-repressor and recruits a co-activator. Co-activators add acetyl tags back to histones, loosening the DNA so transcription starts. Other family members sense lipids like fatty acids or bile acids. In this route, a nuclear receptor binds both ligand and DNA to control transcription.

scenes.visual: Clean end card on deep slate background displaying one line only in bold white text (size 40), centered: 'A nuclear receptor binds both ligand and DNA to control transcription.'
